sections.content: I built my CV and portfolio the way most self-taught developers in Nepal do — by shipping things. Real projects, real clients, real bugs at 2 AM. It worked well enough to get me an interview for a mid-level Laravel role that wanted 4+ years of experience. I had 1.5.
I told myself the portfolio would speak for itself. And it did — it got me in the room. What happened after that is the part nobody warns you about.
Startup taught me everything and nothing

Coming from a startup background, you learn to do everything. You initialize services in constructors because that's what worked. You pull data with `getAttribute` because it gets the job done. You connect two or three databases because the client needed it — a SaaS platform for schools, where every academic year's batch of student data lived in its own separate database, switched dynamically through the config layer.
You solve real problems. But nobody in a startup stops to tell you what any of it is called.

So when I sat down for the interview — a corporate one, my first — and the interviewer (helped along by AI probing deeper into my answers) asked about **dependency injection**, I froze for half a second before realizing: I already do this. I just never knew the term for it. Same story with **mutators** — I knew exactly how to transform an attribute before it hit the database, I just knew it by what it did, not by its name.
That's the strange part of being self-taught in a startup: you're fluent in the practice and illiterate in the vocabulary.
Three interviews taught me more than 1.5 years of work

Here's the part that actually stung, in a good way: those interview rounds forced me to articulate, defend, and name things I'd been doing on instinct for a year and a half. In the space of three conversations, I learned more about why my multi-database setup worked the way it did than I had in all the months I spent building it.

Startups make you hungry for everything. You touch frontend, backend, deployment, client calls — all of it. But you master nothing, because there's no time to stop and go deep. You just ship, and move to the next fire.
The plot twist: corporate wasn't the scary part

I expected corporate to be rigid and intimidating. What I found instead was calm. Clear sprints. Defined tasks. Actual documented standards instead of "just ask so-and-so how we usually do it." The chaos I was used to was the startup. The structure I feared turned out to be a relief.
Nobody tells you that when you're staring down your first corporate interview from inside a startup bubble.
The thing that actually scared me wasn't the tech

Here's what really got me: I didn't know what an HR round even was. Not the questions, not the format, not the purpose — nothing. When the message came through asking me to schedule one, my honest first move was texting HR to ask... for the location. That was the extent of my preparation, because I genuinely didn't know what else to prepare for.

I wasn't unprepared for the work. I was unprepared for the process — the parts of a corporate hiring pipeline that nobody teaches you when your entire career so far has been "get hired by a founder over a coffee chat."
What I'd tell my past self

items: **Learn the vocabulary, not just the skill.** You probably already know more formal concepts than you think — you just know them by what they do, not what they're called. Spend an evening mapping your instincts to their real names.
**Corporate structure isn't the enemy.** It's often less chaotic than what you're used to. Don't walk in bracing for a fight.
**The hiring process has stages you've never seen before.** HR rounds, technical rounds, culture-fit conversations — each one tests something different. Nobody hands you this map. You have to ask.
**Interviews are a form of accelerated learning.** Even the ones that don't end in an offer will teach you more, faster, than another few months of solo shipping.

sections.content: Being a self-taught junior developer in Nepal, chasing roles above your "official" experience level, is its own kind of pressure. The gap between what you can build and what you can explain is real — but it's also closeable, if you know where to look before you're sitting across from an interviewer trying to name something you've been doing all along.
